A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RelayFormer study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A and B are readable, and moved or renumbered material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original image/video localization experiments, component ablations, robustness tests, and qualitative analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds CAT-protocol comparisons, joint image/video training experiments, and further component ablations.

M1.justification: The input partitioning, GLRA token exchange, 4D RoPE, shared backbone with separate adaptations, query-based decoder, and losses remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A.2. Additional implementation explanations and joint-training experiments do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: V3 adds Fantastic Reality and TampCOCO to mixed image training and introduces video-splicing training and evaluation in Section 4.2, extending the previous video-inpainting coverage. MOSE100 matches the previously described 100-clip MOSE test subset. AutoSplice, CocoGlide, and Defacto-12k evaluations remain, despite removing Defacto from the dataset overview.

E2.justification: APSC-Net newly participates in the CAT comparison in Table 1, alongside TruFor, SparseViT, and Mesorch. VideoFACT is removed from Table 2. The MVSS-protocol and Appendix A.6 comparator sets remain unchanged. FOCAL becomes Focal with the same citation and scores, indicating a labeling change.

E3.justification: V3 introduces CAT mixed-dataset training with IMD2020 excluded from testing, six image/video training configurations, and new positional-encoding and partition-size controls. The reported video sub-image size changes from 224×224 to 256×256 in Section 4 and Appendix A.4; unchanged video scores do not establish whether experiments were rerun. The main metrics, threshold, and 200-epoch budget remain.

E4.justification: V3 retains the earlier component, temporal, resolution, corruption, and layer-placement analyses. It adds cross-domain training interactions in Table 4, an ablation disabling 4D RoPE in Table 13, and sub-image size/overlap comparisons in Table 14. Figure 6 adds three-token attention maps supporting the redundancy analysis.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix A.4 states that results are medians of three runs with different seeds. V3 removes this statement and retains only random seed 42 in Table 11. This reduces repeated-run and aggregation disclosure without establishing that fewer runs were performed. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial result entries: CAT average F1 scores are 0.702/0.705 for Relay-ViT/Relay-Seg versus 0.691 for APSC-Net, and Table 4 reports splice F1 of 0.476 with image-plus-splice training versus 0.264 with splice-only training. Tables 13–14 add RoPE and partition results, although Table 13's averages do not match its displayed columns. Earlier MVSS scores and surviving video entries remain numerically unchanged; VideoFACT entries disappear. The added scores are not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: Appendix A.8 removes the premise that N typically dominates m and the associated assertion that local attention has asymptotic cost comparable to standard sub-image attention. The explicit local/global complexity bounds, method equations, and LoRA expressions remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: V2 presents image/video unification as bridging different modalities. V3 explicitly treats them as one visual modality and reframes the contribution as extending spatial modeling to temporal inputs through a single architecture. Resolution adaptivity, efficient relay-based reasoning, and strong localization performance remain the central claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds substantive interpretations of asymmetric image/video transfer and its dependence on shared manipulation types, attributing the asymmetry to dataset diversity and annotation quality. Appendices A.5 and A.7 add token-competition, RoPE-stability, and partition-size explanations. V3 removes the specific hierarchical/convolutional-backbone explanation in A.6. The cross-partition limitation in A.1 remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 specifies the ViT variant, equal dimensional allocation across RoPE axes, and training-resolution bounds. It omits explicit LoRA application to feed-forward networks, validation-based checkpoint selection, and the no-post-processing statement. The supplementary code/video submission note also disappears, while the public code URL remains. Most hyperparameters and the 16-pixel overlap are retained, often relocated or tabulated.

R1.justification: Section 2 sharpens comparisons concerning computational cost, compression dependence, and complementarity to contrastive approaches. Added references include Kniaz et al. (2019), three Qu works, Singla et al. (2023), and Yu et al. (2021). These additions refine the established positioning around efficient, resolution-adaptive image/video localization.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution bullets, related-work paragraphs, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Appendix A.4 is reorganized from continuous prose into settings tables and shorter subsections, and the new joint-training section changes the experimental narrative. Author affiliations, contact information, funding text, and conference headers are also revised.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains separate MVSS/CAT blocks, and v3 adds joint-training and ablation tables. Two settings tables replace implementation prose, while dataset overview tables lose columns and entries. Figure 6 gains three-token panels. Most other figures retain their content, with several relocated; the substantial presentation changes principally concern table organization and added displays.

improvement.justification: The joint-training experiments directly strengthen evidence for the unified-framework motivation, while the new RoPE and partition ablations improve support for design choices. The revised image/video framing is also more precise. These gains are tempered by lost repeated-run and checkpoint-selection disclosures and unexplained averaging in Table 13, yielding a limited net improvement in paper quality.
